title: Some Trees Make City Air Quality Worse — Study
paragraphs: Planting trees is often seen as one of the best ways to improve life in cities, as they provide shade and help clean the air. However, a new study suggests that certain types of trees may actually make air quality worse, particularly during hot weather.

The study, published in the journal Science Advances in August 2026, was carried out by researchers from the University of Innsbruck in Austria and Jinan University in China. They measured the chemicals released into the air in Beijing between May and July 2021, using equipment installed on a 102-meter-tall weather tower. The researchers then traced these chemicals, known as volatile organic compounds, to sources such as trees, traffic, cooking and household products.

Some trees release a chemical called isoprene. When isoprene reacts with nitrogen oxides, which come mainly from traffic and industry, it can produce ground-level ozone, a harmful air pollutant. The researchers found that although trees produced only about a tenth of the volatile organic compounds measured in Beijing, they were responsible for nearly half of the compounds' chemical reactivity, which affects how much ozone is formed. More than 90% of this came from isoprene.

Heat made the problem much worse. As the temperature rose from 20 to 35 degrees Celsius, the reactivity of the chemicals released by trees increased seven- to eight-fold. In contrast, chemicals from human activities became only about 40% more reactive.

According to the study, around 35% of Beijing's trees belong to species that release isoprene, such as weeping willows and Chinese white poplars. When the researchers compared more than 20 cities around the world, they found that isoprene emissions varied more than tenfold, depending largely on the share of these trees.

However, the researchers stressed that cities should not cut down trees or reduce green spaces. As co-author Thomas Karl explained, the findings do not call for less urban greening or the removal of mature trees. Instead, they recommend that cities consider how much isoprene a species releases when choosing which trees to plant. In Beijing, replacing high-emitting trees with low-emitting species in just a tenth of the city's trees during routine replacement could reduce isoprene emissions by at least 29%.
The researchers also emphasized that reducing nitrogen oxide pollution remains essential.
